**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Preserve precise low-value prices in API responses**

For any newly supported price below 0.00005 (including `0.000002891` from the added test), this column now stores the value, but `app/views/api/v1/security_prices/_security_price.json.jbuilder:6` still emits `price_amount` via `format("%.4f", ...)`, producing `"0.0000"`. That field is documented as the exact decimal price in `spec/swagger_helper.rb:1768`, so API consumers still see the asset as worthless; serialize the stored precision and cover the endpoint rather than only asserting the model reload.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

🌐 Web query:

`official PostgreSQL documentation numeric precision scale ALTER TABLE ALTER COLUMN TYPE existing values`

💡 Result:

````
Official PostgreSQL docs say you can change a column’s precision and scale with `ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE`, for example:

```sql
ALTER TABLE products
  ALTER COLUMN price TYPE numeric(10,2);
```

PostgreSQL converts existing values to the new type. A reduced scale rounds values to the specified number of decimal places; if a value then exceeds the allowed precision, the conversion fails. ([postgresql.org](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/ddl-alter.html?utm_source=openai))

The `ALTER TABLE` reference explains that, if needed, `USING` lets you specify how to compute each new value from the old one. ([postgresql.org](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-altertable.htm?utm_source=openai))

Citations:

- 1: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/ddl-alter.html?utm_source=openai
- 2: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-altertable.htm?utm_source=openai
````

**Preserve the existing price range.**

`decimal(19,4)` allows 15 whole-number digits. `decimal(19,10)` allows only 9. Both models permit prices of at least `1,000,000,000`.

When `change_column` converts existing PostgreSQL values, either table can cause the migration to fail if it contains such a price. Increase precision to 25, or establish that the narrower range is acceptable.

**(a) Migration precision/scale (`precision: 25, scale: 10`) — confirmed correct.** The original columns were `decimal(19,4)`, i.e. 15 whole-number digits + 4 fractional. `decimal(25,10)` preserves exactly 15 whole-number digits (25 − 10 = 15) while extending the fractional part to 10, matching `trades.price`'s scale. Note `trades.price` itself is only `decimal(19,10)` (9 whole-number digits) — so this PR is actually *more* correct than the precedent it cites, not just consistent with it. The new `test/models/security/price_test.rb` case for `"123456789012345.25"` (15 whole digits) is a good regression check for this.

**(b) Lossy `down` migration — still unfixed, MAJOR, agree with CodeRabbit.** As of `feb6cdb`, `down` still does `change_column ... decimal, precision: 19, scale: 4`, which will silently truncate any value stored with >4 fractional digits (e.g. `0.000002891` → `0.0000`) on rollback. The author acknowledged this in a comment (11:01 UTC) and offered to switch to raising `ActiveRecord::IrreversibleMigration`, citing `IncreaseCoinbaseBalancePrecision` as the precedent for that pattern — but no follow-up commit has landed yet. This stays entirely in `BigDecimal`/`String` and never round-trips through `Float`. I traced it through the low-value (`0.000002891`), whole-number (`215` → `215.0000`), and max-precision (`12345678.1234567891`) cases and it produces the expected output in each; the new controller tests cover the first and last of these directly.
